Spatial perception were measured via electroencephalography (EEG), using relative alpha power (RA) as an indicator of relaxation.
Psychological responses were assessed through self-reported spatial perception and satisfaction. Results showed
that blue with low-value and high-chroma elicited the highest RA, indicating greater neurophysiological
relaxation, while blue with high-value and low-chroma received the most positive psychological ratings. In
contrast, red with low-value and high-chroma showed lower RA and reduced psychological comfort. These
findings suggest that blue, regardless of value and chroma, supports emotional comfort in learning environments.
Regarding ceiling height, RA peaked at 5 m, while psychological responses were highest at 4 m, after which both
responses declined. A significant correlation between the two was observed only at 4 m. These findings suggest
that a ceiling height of 4 to 5 m may offer a balanced condition for both neural relaxation and emotional comfort,
emphasizing the role of spatial proportion and perception. This study provides empirical evidence on how
environmental attributes such as color and ceiling height modulate neurophysiological and psychological re-
sponses, offering design implications for enhancing learning spaces.

more refined tonal differences, particularly those defined by the inter-
action of value and chroma, remain underexplored. Our study contrib-
utes to filling this gap by demonstrating that even within the same hue,
different tonal compositions can lead to distinct emotional and neuro-
physiological responses.
Meanwhile, psychological responses to color did not fully align with
neurophysiological responses, with no significant correlations were
observed. This discrepancy may be attributed to the fundamentally
different nature of these response types. Neurophysiological reactions,
such as changes in relative alpha power, reflect immediate, automatic
sensory processes initiated by bottom-up input from the sensory organs
to the primary sensory cortex (e.g., the visual cortex) [79]. However,
these responses may not directly or consistently translate into psycho-
logical outcomes. In contrast, psychological responses are shaped
through more complex, top-down processes involving cognitive
appraisal, prior experiences, and subjective interpretation [80,81].
These differences imply that sensory perception and emotional evalua-
tion of color operate through distinct neural and psychological
mechanisms.
This conceptual divergence was particularly evident in the B2 con-
dition (low value, high chroma blue), where participants exhibited the
highest level of relative alpha power—suggestive of physiological
relaxation—yet reported relatively low levels of subjective relaxation.
This mismatch may reflect how strong chromatic saturation, while
producing cortical disengagement at the neural level, can still be
perceived as visually intense or emotionally overstimulating due to in-
dividual cognitive or affective filters. The B2 case illustrates how the
same sensory stimulus can produce contrasting outcomes depending on
whether the response is measured physiologically or psychologically.
Moreover, this inconsistency may be further explained by differences
in temporal and cognitive dimensions between the two types of mea-
sures. While EEG captures immediate, automatic neural responses dur-
ing stimulus exposure, subjective evaluations are collected after the
experience and are shaped by reflective processes such as aesthetic
judgment, personal expectations, or cognitive biases. These additional
layers of interpretation can modulate the final self-reported outcome
and contribute to the lack of direct correspondence between physio-
logical and psychological data.
Prior research emphasized that color processing begins with bio-
logically universal mechanisms, such as the perception of wavelengths
of light, relatively independent of cultural influence [82]. However, as
sensory input is further processed, individual differences emerge. Psy-
chological interpretations of color are known to be influenced by a wide
range of factors, including cultural background, environmental context
[83], age, gender, and even geographical location [84]. Furthermore,
studies suggest that the mechanisms underlying color preference and
affective evaluation differ from those responsible for basic perceptual
responses [85]. This layered complexity may explain why neurophysi-
ological indicators of sensory relaxation do not always align with sub-
jective reports of emotional satisfaction. While the brain may exhibit
consistent neural patterns in response to specific color properties, the
subjective experience of color is modulated by interpretive processes
that extend beyond immediate sensory input. These findings highlight
the need for a multidimensional approach in color-related research,
incorporating both physiological and psychological perspectives to
better understand user experience in spatial environments.
In this context, while LVHC blue may elicit greater sensory relaxation
as indicated by elevated RA, HVLC blue is more likely to be perceived as
pleasant and satisfying in a learning environment, due to its softer and
lighter tone. This distinction highlights the importance of considering
both physiological and psychological dimensions when evaluating the
effects of color in spatial design, as they may not always align but offer
complementary insights into users’ experiences.
Taken together, the findings suggest that blue tones, regardless of
chromatic variation, are effective in promoting relaxation and comfort.
